All the three issues have been decided by the Commission against the Appellant in the impugned order and hence the Appellant is before us in this appeal. 11. We have heard Learned Counsel for the Appellant as well as Learned Counsel for Respondent Nos. 4 to 7. No other respondents contested the appeal. We have also gone through the impugned order and the written submissions filed by the Learned Counsels. instructions to the Appellant, therefore, the delay in complying with the condition occasioned only due to the internal hierarchy in the 2[nd] Respondent Company. It is his submission that the Appellant has been unjustly held accountable for internal departmental mis-communications between the officers of the 2[nd] Respondent- BESCOM despite there being no direct communication to her to comply with the conditions set out by the Commission while approving the PPA. He would argue that non-submission of requisite documents to the Commission within 15 days of approval letter dated 1[st] January, 2016 was solely on account of the failure on the part of the officials of BESCOM for which the Appellant cannot be held responsible. He also submitted that no prior notice was issued to the Appellant before informing her that the PPA dated 11[th] December, 2016 had lapsed. Learned Counsel cited the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Venkatraman Krishnamurthy & Anr. Vs. Lodha Crown Buildmart Pvt. Ltd. in Civil Appeal No. 971 of 2023 decided on 22[nd] February, 2024 to canvass that the contract is to be interpreted while quoting the actual meaning to the words contained in it and it is not permissible for court to amend or re-write a new contract, Union of India and Ors. Vs. Hindustan Development Corpn. and Ors.(1993) 3 SCC 499 to canvass that the Court has power to lift the veil and see whether the decision is violative of principle of natural justice, arbitrary of - unreasonable; Navjyoti Coo Group Housing Society and Ors. Vs. Union of India (UOI) and Ors., (1992) 4 SCC 477, to canvass that the doctrine of legitimate expectation imposes a duty on public authority to act fairly by considering all relevant factors before taking a decision. 15. We have considered the rival submissions made by the Learned Counsels and have perused the entire record. 17. It is the case of the Appellant that she had submitted the requisite documents in this regard to the 2[nd] Respondent even before the issue of letter dated 1[st] January, 2016 by the Commission. We do not find any force in the said contention of the Appellant. The details of the documents i.e. proof of the existence of available roof top space admeasuring 9700 sq.mts., said to have been submitted by the Appellant to the 2[nd] Respondent, have nowhere been given either in the proceedings before the Commission or in the memo of appeal filed before this Tribunal. Even if we take the said contention of the Appellant on its face value that she had already submitted the requisite documents to the 2[nd] Respondent, that did not absolve her from complying with the condition specified by the Commission while approving the PPA. She knew that the approval accorded to the PPA was conditional and, therefore, ought to have either complied with the condition herself or called upon the 2[nd] Respondent to comply with the condition. She did not do either. Therefore, it does not terms. In the absence of the approved PPA, the Respondents were not required to seek its termination by issuance of default notice under the provisions of the PPA. Since the condition specified by the Commission while approving the PPA has remained to be complied with either by the Appellant or by the 2[nd] Respondent, the approval lapsed and the PPA became unenforceable. Therefore, the 2[nd] Respondent was not obligated to follow the procedure specified in the PPA for its termination as the PPA ceased to exist on account of lapse of the approval accorded to it by the Commission. Reliance placed on behalf of the Appellant in this regard on the judgement of the Apex Court in Venkataraman Krishnamurthy case (supra) is wholly misplaced for the reason that neither has the Commission nor is this Tribunal amending or re-writing the contract between the Appellant and the 2[nd] Respondent. The Commission has held that PPA ceased to exist on account of failure on the part of the Appellant or the 2[nd] Respondent to fulfill the conditions specified by the Commission while approving the same, which seems to be perfectly sound and legally tenable. Therefore, no agreement subsisted between the Appellant and 2[nd] Respondent at all and the question of amending or re-writing any such agreement did not arise at all. 21. The judgements of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Hindustan Development Corpn. Case (Supra) and Navjyoti Coo-Group Housing case (supra) cited by the Learned Counsel for the Appellant are also not relevant to the facts and circumstances of the instant case. We may note at the cost of repetition that the Appellant had knowledge of the conditional approval accorded by the Commission to the PPA and, therefore, it was her responsibility to either fulfill the condition herself or call upon the 2[nd] Respondent to fulfill the same. Since she failed to do either of the two, her contention of legitimate expectation is not tenable. 22. In view of the above discussion, we do not find any error or infirmity in the impugned order of the Commission. The appeal is devoid of any merit and is hereby dismissed.
